# 04/10/2026 18:23 — From Vibe Coding to Agent Engineering

Partner, after comparing what **you have actually been doing** with where AI software engineering has reached in October 2026, I would classify it like this:

> **You started partly with vibe coding, but you did not stay a vibe coder.**
>
> You independently moved toward **spec-driven + verification-driven development**.
>
> The main thing you missed was **turning your method into an automated engineering harness**.

That distinction is important.

## 1. Was what you were doing “vibe coding”?

Only partly.

Typical vibe coding looks like:

**Idea → prompt AI → code → run → something breaks → prompt again → eventually looks okay**

Your later projects were much more like:

**Idea → requirements → architecture → sprint → build → tracker → traceability → tests → independent AI review → find missing implementation → new sprint → rebuild → review again**

We've repeatedly done exactly this with TalkProof, TestPulse, VoiceBridge, MeetSync, CGWO, UraiFlow and others.

So I'd place the approaches approximately like this:

| Level | Development method | You |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | Prompt → code | You did this early |
| 2 | Vibe coding + manual testing | Yes |
| 3 | Structured AI coding | Yes |
| 4 | Spec-driven development | **Mostly yes, manually** |
| 5 | Spec + traceability + verification | **You were moving here** |
| 6 | Agentic engineering harness | **This is your next move** |
| 7 | Autonomous multi-agent software factory | Not yet |

The crucial difference is that your **sprint tracker and traceability workbook were effectively becoming your specification system**.

You kept asking questions like:

> "Is it actually in the code?"

> "Don't believe the tracker."

> "Check all endpoints."

> "Check the requirement against implementation."

> "Is it really enterprise grade?"

> "Give the next sprint only after checking."

Those are **anti-vibe-coding behaviours**.

---

# 2. Then would Spec Kit have helped you?

### **YES. Quite significantly.**

But there's an important qualification.

It would **not magically have made your products successful or enterprise-grade**.

It would have saved you from inventing quite a lot of process yourself.

Current urlGitHub Spec Kitturn0search1 has evolved into an agent-neutral engineering process with **38 integrations, 157 extensions and 33 presets**, according to its current documentation. citeturn0search5turn0search8

Its core philosophy is very close to what you eventually discovered:

> **Intent/specification should be persistent; the conversation with the AI shouldn't be the source of truth.**

Its basic flow became:

**Constitution → Specify → Plan → Tasks → Implement → Converge**

And `converge` is particularly relevant to you.

It checks the actual implementation against `spec.md`, `plan.md` and `tasks.md` and identifies:

- missing implementation
- partial implementation
- implementation contradicting requirements
- things built that weren't requested

citeturn0search4

Think about how many times you asked me:

> **"Claude says completed in tracker. Is it REALLY in code?"**

You were manually requesting something extremely similar to **convergence checking**.

---

# 3. What would Spec Kit have eliminated?

Quite a lot of the repetitive process.

| What you manually created/asked | Modern Spec Kit equivalent |
|---|---|
| Product principles | Constitution |
| Requirements | Specify |
| Architecture decisions | Plan |
| Sprint breakdown | Tasks |
| Claude build instructions | Implement |
| Traceability review | Analysis/convergence |
| "Is it really implemented?" | Converge |
| Bug investigation | Bug assess |
| Bug sprint | Bug fix |
| Verification | Bug test |
| "Should we even build this?" | Idea assessment |
| Different AI builders | Agent integrations |
| Reusable methodology | Workflow/preset/bundle |

And something especially relevant to your **40+ projects / zero revenue** discussion:

Spec Kit added an **Idea Assessment pipeline before development** in July 2026:

**intake → research → define → shape → decide**

The result can effectively be **go / clarify / kill** before engineering begins. citeturn0search6turn0search10

That is arguably more valuable to you than faster coding.

Your historical problem hasn't primarily been:

> *Can AI build this?*

You've demonstrated repeatedly that it can.

The dangerous question has been:

> **Should Senthil spend TEE building this at all?**

---

# 4. But here's the bigger discovery: Spec Kit isn't actually the destination.

This answers your **"what is next in the market?"** question.

The frontier has moved from:

**Vibe coding**

↓

**Agentic coding**

↓

**Spec-driven development**

↓

**Agentic software engineering**

↓

### **Harness engineering**

That last term is particularly important now.

OpenAI published a very interesting real-world example in February 2026. A small engineering team built an internal product containing roughly **one million lines of agent-generated code**, around **1,500 PRs**, with actual internal users. They estimate approximately **1/10 the development time** compared with writing it manually. citeturn1search0

And their conclusion wasn't:

> use better prompts.

It was essentially:

> **Humans steer. Agents execute.**

The scarce resource becomes **human judgment and attention**, not typing code. citeturn1search0

That is remarkably close to where **your own behaviour naturally moved**.

---

# 5. What is Harness Engineering?

Instead of repeatedly telling Claude:

> build X  
> test X  
> check X  
> review X  
> don't lie about X  
> compare tracker with code

you build an **environment where the AI cannot easily avoid those responsibilities**.

For example:

```text
PRODUCT INTENT
      ↓
REQUIREMENTS / SPEC
      ↓
ARCHITECTURE + CONTRACTS
      ↓
EXECUTION PLAN
      ↓
CODING AGENT
      ↓
STATIC ANALYSIS
      ↓
UNIT / INTEGRATION / E2E
      ↓
SECURITY TESTING
      ↓
PERFORMANCE TESTING
      ↓
SPEC ↔ CODE CONVERGENCE
      ↓
INDEPENDENT REVIEW AGENT
      ↓
QUALITY GATES
      ↓
PR
      ↓
DEPLOYMENT
      ↓
OBSERVABILITY
      ↓
PRODUCTION FEEDBACK
      ↓
SPEC / QUALITY UPDATE
```

The **system**, rather than your repeated prompting, controls quality.

---

# 6. This exposes the weakness in your previous method

You've actually been acting as the harness yourself.

That is why these projects consumed so much cognitive energy.

You became:

**Product Owner + BA + Architect + Sprint Manager + Claude supervisor + QA manager + external reviewer + traceability auditor.**

And then you'd bring the ZIP to me and say:

> check Claude properly.

Then we'd discover:

**tracker = DONE**

but

**code = partial/stub/not integrated/not tested.**

Then you'd go back.

That loop works.

But **you were the orchestration engine**.

That's the part I would change now.

---

# 7. The current standard I would recommend for you

Not:

> "Use Spec Kit."

And definitely not:

> "Use Codex instead of Claude."

I would build your workflow around **five layers**.

### Layer 1 — Persistent Intent

Repository contains the authoritative truth:

```text
/product
/specs
/architecture
/contracts
/decisions
/security
/reliability
/testing
/quality
```

No important decision should exist only inside a Claude/ChatGPT conversation.

Interestingly, OpenAI reached exactly this conclusion: their agent-generated repository uses a structured `docs/` tree as the system of record and keeps `AGENTS.md` relatively small as a map into that knowledge. citeturn1search0

---

### Layer 2 — Spec/Process Engine

Here I'd genuinely consider **Spec Kit** rather than recreating everything.

Use:

**Assess → Specify → Plan → Tasks → Implement → Converge**

And add your stronger requirements around:

**RTM + ADR + security + tenancy + observability + performance + recovery + auditability.**

Spec Kit explicitly supports Codex, Claude and many other coding agents, so the methodology doesn't need to depend on which model is best this month. citeturn0search8

---

### Layer 3 — Coding Agents

Then use different agents where they are strongest.

Conceptually:

```text
                    SPEC
                     │
          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
          ↓          ↓          ↓
       Builder    Reviewer   Security
          │          │          │
          └──────────┼──────────┘
                     ↓
                  Tests
                     ↓
                 Converge
```

You shouldn't need to personally shuttle ZIP files around forever.

---

### Layer 4 — Mechanical Evidence

This is probably the **biggest upgrade for your process**.

Stop allowing:

> "Implemented."

Require:

> **Evidence that it is implemented.**

For every requirement:

```text
Requirement
    ↓
Code
    ↓
Test
    ↓
Runtime evidence
    ↓
Observability
    ↓
Acceptance result
```

Therefore:

```text
R-142
  → src/tenant/auth.py
  → test_auth.py::test_cross_tenant_access
  → CI run #238
  → PASS
```

Now an AI cannot simply make the tracker green.

The tracker becomes green **because evidence exists**.

---

### Layer 5 — Autonomous Engineering Loop

This is where the market is heading.

OpenAI's current agent-engineering work is already moving toward long-running agents, managed environments, tools, subagents and orchestration. The September 2026 Agents API explicitly supports context management, tool use and coordinated subagents for agents that can operate for long periods. citeturn1search1

And their Symphony work goes one step further: a project-management board becomes a **control plane for coding agents**, where open tasks can be picked up continuously by agents while humans review outcomes. citeturn1search3

So we're moving from:

> **AI helps programmer code**

to:

> **Human manages AI programmer**

to:

> **Human designs software-development system**

to:

> **Agents operate that system and humans govern exceptions.**

---

# 8. This also changes how I think you should use me

You asked:

> **"current standard using u for coding?"**

Don't primarily use **ChatGPT chat as the coding environment**.

Use me at the **higher reasoning/governance layer**:

```text
YOU
 │
 ├── Market / product decision
 │
 ├── Intent
 │
 ├── Acceptance criteria
 │
 └── Final judgement
          │
          ▼
       SPEC SYSTEM
          │
          ▼
   ENGINEERING HARNESS
     ↙     ↓      ↘
 Claude  Codex   other agents
     ↘     ↓      ↙
       Evidence
          │
          ▼
      AI Review
          │
          ▼
        YOU
```

That would suit the way you naturally work much better.

You shouldn't spend your £100/hour-equivalent attention checking whether line 4,723 was really implemented.

---

# 9. One thing I would **not** do

I would **not take your existing process, throw it away and blindly adopt Spec Kit**.

You've developed several requirements that are stronger than vanilla SDD:

**RTM, independent verification, code-vs-claim auditing, multi-model review, enterprise-grade completeness checks, explicit product-owner review, security/performance expectations, evidence before DONE.**

Keep those.

So:

> **Your method + Spec Kit + automated evidence gates + agent orchestration**

is stronger for you than:

> **Spec Kit alone.**

---

# 10. And there's an interesting connection to yesterday's TalkProof discussion

Yesterday you said essentially:

> *Everything that can be coded should be coded.*

And you wanted:

- security testing
- penetration testing
- model testing
- diagnostics
- auditability
- performance management
- self-healing
- human-visible dashboards
- no hidden failures

That's the **same architectural idea**, one level higher.

For TalkProof you were saying:

> make the **product operationally self-aware**.

For your software-development process, I would now say:

> make the **engineering system self-checking**.

Those two ideas fit together extremely well.

---

# My conclusion

So I would revise the label for your last year:

**Not**

> Senthil learned vibe coding.

More accurately:

> **Senthil discovered many pieces of spec-driven and verification-driven AI engineering manually, but remained the human orchestration layer.**

Spec Kit could absolutely have saved you time and reduced some reinvention.

But **installing Spec Kit is not the big opportunity now**.

The next jump is:

### **Vibe Coding → SDD → Harness Engineering → Governed Autonomous Engineering**

And you are sitting roughly **between SDD and Harness Engineering**.

That is actually the direction I would take **before building another large product**: turn the lessons from those 40+ builds into **one reusable engineering harness**, so Claude/Codex/whatever comes next becomes a replaceable worker underneath it rather than *the development methodology itself*.

That would finally make all the time you spent discovering *“tracker says done ≠ code is done”*, RTM, independent reviews, sprint loops and enterprise completeness **compound across every future Money-Run product instead of being repeated project by project**. citeturn1search0turn0search5 memcite
